analysis.one_liner: Makes oil spillers strictly liable for cleanup costs and damages, with caps, and tightens tanker safety rules.
analysis.headline: Eighteen bipartisan cosponsors backed the bill, but it never got a House vote; its substance was folded into H.R. 1465, which became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the Exxon Valdez spill, the bill would make the company responsible for an oil spill pay for cleanup and for damages to property, livelihoods, and natural resources — with liability caps for the biggest accidents. It would also require spill response plans, tougher tanker and crew standards, and special protections for Prince William Sound, Alaska. This version never got a vote; the House instead passed the same overhaul through H.R. 1465, which became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or fish on or near U.S. waters: the bill lets them recover cleanup costs, lost profits and earnings, property losses, and loss of subsistence resources from the company that spilled the oil [S3]. State, local, and tribal governments gain authority to recover damages to natural resources and to run restoration plans [S3]. Taxpayers gain because the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund is backed by mandatory payments from industry, with the government recovering what it pays out from responsible parties [S3]. Coast Guard-credentialed mariners face new screening, but the public gains drunk- and drug-driving checks on tanker officers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishermen, states, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Makes the responsible party strictly, jointly, and severally liable for oil spill cleanup costs and for damages to property, lost profits and earning capacity, lost tax revenues, and loss of subsistence use of natural resources — so fishermen, small businesses, and coastal homeowners do not have to prove fault or sue under ordinary negligence rules.
Creates a claims process and an Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund that pays claims when the spiller will not, and lets state governors directly obligate up to $250,000 for immediate spill response.
Gives federal, state, and Indian tribe trustees the right to recover natural resource damages and spend the money restoring the damaged resources.

Requires tank vessels and facilities to file approved spill contingency plans before handling oil, mandates escorts and Alaska-licensed pilots for tankers leaving Valdez, and requires a spill-removal capability in Prince William Sound sized to a 200,000-barrel discharge.

Requires financial responsibility (insurance, bonds, or self-insurance) from vessel owners, cargo owners, and offshore facility operators, and lets the government deny port entry, detain, or seize vessels that cannot show it.

analysis.who_pays: The oil shipping and production industry: tanker owners and operators, owners of oil carried as cargo, offshore facility operators, and Trans-Alaska Pipeline right-of-way holders would bear strict liability, civil penalties, financial responsibility requirements, and spill-preparation costs [S3]. Vessel crews face alcohol/driving-record screening and license suspension or revocation for alcohol- or drug-related offenses [S2]. Some costs would ultimately reach consumers through shipping and insurance rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil tanker, cargo, and offshore facility owners

drawbacks.text: Liability is capped — for a large tank vessel at the greater of $1,200 per gross ton or $10 million, and for most other facilities at $350 million — so victims and the Fund absorb the enormous costs of catastrophes that exceed the caps; Exxon Valdez-scale damages ran far beyond limits like these.

The bill preempts most state-court claims arising from a spill (except personal injury) and bars states from requiring any additional proof of financial responsibility, reducing the ability of coastal states to write tougher rules than the federal floor.
Challenges to the bill's regulations go only to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, concentrating review in a single court far from most affected communities.
Liability does not apply to discharges made under a federal, state, or local permit, or from government-owned vessels, leaving those sources of pollution outside the compensation scheme.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the bill is strongly net positive: it shifts spill costs onto the companies that create the risk and builds a real response and restoration system. The main concession is the liability cap, which protects the largest players precisely in the worst spills — the Exxon Valdez case shows real damages can dwarf the caps — and the federal preemption of state claims slightly narrows local power. Even with those flaws, the scheme was fair enough that Congress enacted its substance the following year.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and a subcommittee without ever coming to a vote; the House's action list redirects it to H.R. 1465, the companion oil-spill bill that became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 3, 1989, seven months after the Exxon Valdez spill in Prince William Sound, which the bill's own text targets with a dedicated removal and restoration title.

It was referred the same day to three House committees — Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Public Works and Transportation, and Science, Space and Technology — and a week later to the Subcommittee on Water Resources.
It drew 18 cosponsors split evenly between the parties, 9 Democrats and 9 Republicans, but no committee ever reported it.
On November 9, 1989, the House action history states simply 'See H.R.1465', meaning the effort moved to that bill, which Congress passed and which became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, fishermen, and taxpayers ultimately got the liability and spill-prevention regime they wanted through the successor law, while oil shippers and cargo owners secured the part of this bill they needed most: statutory caps limiting their worst-case losses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities; oil shippers kept liability caps

for.name: Walter B. Jones
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-NC); chair of the House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 11 original cosponsors and shepherded it through the committee with jurisdiction over oil spill legislation.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Water Resources
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Public Works and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 16, 1989 and never reported it; the effort moved instead to H.R. 1465.

against.name: Oil and shipping industry interests
against.role: Tanker owners, oil cargo owners, and offshore operators
against.what_they_did: Pressed during the 1989-1990 oil spill debate to keep spiller liability capped rather than unlimited; the bill's cap structure reflects that fight.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan at introduction — 9 Democratic and 9 Republican cosponsors — and the record shows no partisan opposition, only inaction in committee.

industries.note: The bill makes them strictly liable for spills and requires insurance-backed financial responsibility, but it also caps their worst-case losses at the greater of $1,200 per gross ton or $10 million per incident, except for gross negligence or regulation violations. The cap protects them exactly where the public is most exposed, as Exxon Valdez damages showed.

industries.industry: Oil producers and offshore facility operators
industries.note: They face strict liability up to $350 million, a $150 million financial responsibility requirement, higher penalties, and mandatory spill contingency plans; Trans-Alaska Pipeline right-of-way holders would pay state cleanup administration costs. Their loss is the public's gain in cleanup and restoration funding.

The bill obliges vessel, cargo, and facility owners to buy evidence of financial responsibility — insurance, surety bonds, guarantees, or letters of credit — creating a large new market for underwriters, though guarantors face direct claims up to their coverage.

The bill lets them recover lost profits and earning capacity from a spill without proving fault, and funds restoration of the fisheries and shorelines they depend on; Prince William Sound's fishing communities get dedicated equipment and training provisions.
